levelDesc.moderada: There are solid studies, but few in real life, or results that do not always agree.
levelDesc.preliminar: The idea is reasonable and there are signs, but good studies confirming it are still missing.

beforeChat.title: You first, the AI second
beforeChat.goal: Answer a question with your own head before you look it up with an AI or Google.
steps: Think of something you really want to know: about work, home, or plain curiosity.
Tap “Start” and write the question the way you'd ask the AI.
Write your best answer, even if you're not sure, and mark how sure you are. Then tap “Save my attempt”.
beforeChat.example: Question: “How often should you water a cactus?” Your attempt: “About once a month, because it can handle drought.” Sure: 2 out of 5.
beforeChat.done: when you save your attempt. It marks itself.
beforeChat.why: Trying to answer before you see the answer, even if you get it wrong, makes you remember it much better later.

sayIt.title: Guess before you search
sayIt.goal: Next time you're about to look up a fact on your phone, say your answer first.
steps: Today, when a question pops up (a date, a fact, how to do something), don't look it up yet.
Say out loud, or jot on paper, what you think the answer is.
Now look it up and see how close you were.
sayIt.example: “What year did people land on the Moon?” You say: “1972.” You check: it was 1969. Close!
sayIt.done: when you've done all three once: guess, look up and compare.
sayIt.why: Risking an answer before seeing it makes the fact stick better, even when you're wrong.

solveAlone.title: One problem, no help
solveAlone.goal: Solve a real work or study problem on your own, and use the AI only to compare at the end.
steps: Pick a problem from today that you'd normally hand to the AI: a tricky email, an exercise, a work question.
Work on it alone for at least 15 minutes, on paper or in your head.
Tap “Start”, write the problem and your solution, and save it.
If you like, ask the AI at the end and compare.
solveAlone.example: Problem: “How do we share out the team's holidays without overlaps?” Your solution: a table of months where everyone picks in turns.
solveAlone.done: when you save your solution in Think first. It marks itself.
solveAlone.why: The effort of solving something yourself is exactly what keeps the skill alive; if someone else always does it, it rusts.

explain.title: Tell someone about it
explain.goal: Explain from memory something you learned this week.
steps: Pick something you learned or read recently: a news story, a recipe, something from work.
Tell someone about it (in person, on a call or in a voice note) without looking at notes or your phone.
Afterwards, check where you got it from and notice what you forgot or got wrong.
explain.example: You tell a friend what you read on Monday about new traffic fines, then notice you forgot the amount.
explain.done: when you've finished explaining and checked what you missed.
explain.why: Pulling what you learned out of memory fixes it far better than reading it again.

agenda.title: Your day from memory
agenda.goal: Recall what you have on today before you look at your calendar.
steps: Before opening your planner or calendar, stop for a moment.
Say or write everything you have today: appointments, to-dos and times.
Open the calendar and compare. What did you miss?
agenda.example: “Meeting at 10, pick up the kids at 3, pay the power bill.” The calendar says you also had the dentist at 5.
agenda.done: when you've compared your list with the calendar.
agenda.why: Every time you try to recall something before looking, your memory gets practice. Looking first doesn't.

shopping.title: Shop from memory
shopping.goal: Do the shopping remembering your list, without taking it out.
steps: Write your list as usual and read it through once, calmly.
Put it in your pocket and shop without taking it out.
Before paying, check the list for anything missing.
shopping.example: A list of 8 things: you remember 7. Before paying you see you forgot the coffee and go get it.
shopping.done: when you've shopped without looking at the list and checked it only at the end.
shopping.why: Trying to recall the list is real practice: each attempt makes it stick better.

greet.title: Call them by name
greet.goal: Greet someone you met recently by their name.
steps: Think of someone you met recently: a neighbor, someone from work or church.
Before you see them, recall their name. If you saved them in People's names, go over it there.
Greet them using their name.
greet.example: “Morning, Andrew! How did the move go?”
greet.done: when you've greeted someone using their name.
greet.why: Saying a name out loud is real practice. And people are glad to be remembered.

register.title: A new name
register.goal: Learn the name of someone you meet today.
steps: When you're introduced to someone, repeat their name in the conversation: “Nice to meet you, Laura.”
Notice something that sets them apart and something you talked about.
Afterwards, tap “Start” and save them. The app guides you to create a picture that helps you remember the name.
register.example: Laura, red glasses, works at a bakery. Picture: a giant laurel wreath wearing red glasses, coming out of the oven.
register.done: when you save the person in the app. It marks itself.
register.why: Linking a name to an exaggerated picture is a technique for remembering names that has been studied for decades.

meeting.title: Go over who's coming
meeting.goal: Before a get-together with several people, go over their names.
steps: Before a meeting, class or meal with several people, find one minute.
Without looking at anything, say the name of everyone who'll be there.
If one escapes you, find it out and use it during the get-together.
meeting.example: Parents' meeting: “Caroline, George, Ms. Ines…” You can't recall Tom's dad; you find out and greet him by name.
meeting.done: when you've gone over the names and used at least one.
meeting.why: Recalling names just before you need them is well-timed practice, which is when it helps most.

plan.title: A trip without GPS
plan.goal: Make one of today's trips guided only by what you planned before leaving.
steps: Pick a real trip for today, ideally one you don't know well.
Tap “Start”, look at the map and write down 3 to 6 places you'll pass: a park, a gas station, where you turn.
Make the trip without GPS. If you get lost, ask someone or glance at the map for a second.
When you arrive, open the route in the app and say how it went.
plan.example: Home → new clinic: the church, right at the pharmacy, on to the bridge, blue building.
plan.done: when you report how it went without having followed the GPS. It marks itself.
plan.why: Finding your own way works the part of the brain that builds your mental map. Following GPS barely uses it.

return.title: Another way home
return.goal: Go home by a different way, without looking at the map.
steps: Today, on your way home, change part of your usual route. Do it in daylight and in an area you know.
Go by what you know: which way home is, the big streets, places you recognize.
Look at the map only if you're really lost.
return.example: Instead of taking the avenue, you take the street by the park and come out two blocks further on.
return.done: when you got home by another way without following the map.
return.why: Finding a new route by yourself widens your mental map; always repeating the same one doesn't.

landmarks.title: Five signs on the way
landmarks.goal: Notice what you see on a trip you always make.
steps: On a trip you make often, look for 5 things that can serve as signs: a big tree, a billboard, a mural.
When you arrive, write them down in order on paper or in your notes.
Next time you pass by, check whether the order was right.
landmarks.example: Corner bakery, long traffic light, yellow church, bridge, gas station.
landmarks.done: when you've written down the 5 signs in order.
landmarks.why: People with a good sense of direction pay attention to landmarks. It's a habit you learn by practicing it.

pointHome.title: Which way is home?
pointHome.goal: Guess which way home is from a new place.
steps: When you leave a place you don't often go to, stop for a moment.
Without looking at your phone, point toward where you think home is.
Now open the map and check. How close were you?
pointHome.example: You leave a mall and point left. The map says it was almost straight ahead: you were a bit off.
pointHome.done: when you've pointed and checked it on the map.
pointHome.why: Guessing and checking is the most direct way to sharpen your sense of direction.

message.title: In your own words
message.goal: Write an important message without AI and without keyboard suggestions.
steps: Pick a message from today that matters to you: congratulations, an apology, a reply to your boss.
Write it yourself from start to finish, without asking the AI and without tapping the words your keyboard suggests.
Read it once, fix whatever you like, and send it.
message.example: A birthday message for your aunt that isn't just “Happy birthday!”, but something only you would say to her.
message.done: when you've sent a message written entirely by you.
message.why: Writing is thinking: putting your ideas in order in your own words is the skill you lose if someone else always writes.

email.title: Your draft first
email.goal: Write a real email yourself first, before asking for help.
steps: Think of an email you need to send today or tomorrow.
Tap “Start” and then “New draft”. Write the whole email (pasting text is off here).
Tap “Finish draft”. If you like, compare it afterwards with what an AI would suggest.
email.example: An email asking your landlord to fix the shower: greeting, what's wrong, since when, and what you're asking for.
email.done: when you finish the draft in the app. It marks itself.
email.why: If you write first, the AI becomes a second opinion instead of the one doing your thinking.

summary.title: Sum it up without looking
summary.goal: Write in your own words the main points of something you read or watched today.
steps: Pick something you read or watched today: an article, a chapter, a video, a class.
Close it. Tap “Start”, then “New draft”, and write the main points in 5 to 10 lines without looking back.
Tap “Finish draft” and then check the original: what did you miss?
summary.example: An article about sleep: “Sleeping under 7 hours hurts memory. Phone light delays sleep. Going to bed at the same time helps.”
summary.done: when you finish the draft in the app. It marks itself.
summary.why: Summarizing from memory makes you recall and organize the ideas: two of the best-proven ways to learn.

groceries.title: The total before the till
groceries.goal: Know what you'll pay for your shopping before you're told.
steps: While you shop, keep a running total in your head. Round it: $2.95 is $3.
Before paying, say your total.
Compare it with what the till shows.
groceries.example: Bread $3 + milk $4.50 + eggs $5 + coffee $9 = about $21.50. The till says $21.20.
groceries.done: when you've said your total and compared it with the till.
groceries.why: Doing sums with real money keeps the skill right where you need it.

tip.title: Your share, no calculator
tip.goal: Work out the tip or everyone's share in your head.
steps: When the bill arrives for a meal or an outing, leave the calculator alone.
Work out the tip in your head (10% is moving the decimal point one place) or what each person pays.
If you like, check it on your phone afterwards.
tip.example: An $84 bill split 4 ways: $80 ÷ 4 = $20 and $4 ÷ 4 = $1. Each person pays $21.
tip.done: when you've done the sum in your head before checking it.
tip.why: Breaking a sum into easy pieces is a skill that fades if the calculator always does it.

budget.title: How much did I spend this week?
budget.goal: Work out your spending for the week and see how close you were.
steps: Without checking your bank, go over the week day by day: what you bought and roughly what it cost.
Add it up and write your total.
Open your bank app or receipts and compare.
budget.example: Groceries $120, gas $60, lunches $45… Your total: $260. The bank says $290.
budget.done: when you've written your total and compared it with the real figure.
budget.why: Working it out before looking gives you a feel for amounts, and you also learn where your money goes.

arrival.title: What time will I get there?
arrival.goal: Work out your arrival time in your head before you leave.
steps: Before heading somewhere, work out how long it takes and what time you'll arrive.
Say the time out loud: “I'll get there at 4:25.”
When you arrive, look at the clock and compare.
arrival.example: It's 3:50. The trip is 25 minutes, plus 10 waiting for the bus: 3:50 + 35 minutes = 4:25.
arrival.done: when you've said your arrival time and compared it when you got there.
arrival.why: Adding hours and minutes in your head is an everyday sum the phone habit takes away.

estimate.title: How much do you think it is?
estimate.goal: Guess a price or a figure before looking it up.
steps: Today, before looking up a price or any number, stop.
Say your guess, as specific as you can.
Look up the real figure and see how far off you were.
estimate.example: “How much is a mid-size fridge?” You say $600. The store says $750: a little low.
estimate.done: when you've guessed and checked at least once.
estimate.why: Guessing and checking sharpens your feel for amounts: every miss brings you closer next time.

phone.title: A number by heart
phone.goal: Learn the phone number of someone close to you.
steps: Pick someone important whose number you don't know: your partner, a child, your mom.
Learn it in chunks of 3 or 4 digits, repeating it out loud.
Later on, dial it without opening your contacts.
phone.example: 555 · 201 · 1234: you repeat it three times in the morning and dial it from memory in the afternoon.
phone.done: when you've dialed it without looking at your contacts.
phone.why: Recalling it hours later is what makes it stick. And it helps the day you don't have your phone.

askWay.title: Ask the way
askWay.goal: Get somewhere by asking a person instead of using the map.
steps: Next time you don't know how to get somewhere nearby, put your phone away.
Ask someone: a shopkeeper, a security guard, a neighbor.
Repeat the directions out loud and follow them.
askWay.example: “Two blocks straight, left at the pharmacy, and it's the white building.” You: “Two straight, pharmacy, left, white.”
askWay.done: when you've arrived following someone's directions.
askWay.why: Following spoken directions makes you build the map in your head, exactly what GPS does for you.

teach.title: Teach someone
teach.goal: Teach someone something you know how to do, without looking anything up.
steps: Think of something you do well: a recipe, a phone trick, changing a tire.
Explain it to someone step by step, without watching videos or reading instructions.
Ask them to do it or repeat it back, to see whether you explained it well.
teach.example: You teach your nephew to make pancakes: flour, eggs, milk, mix, pour, flip.
teach.done: when the other person could do it or repeat it.
teach.why: Explaining something from memory makes you recall and organize it; that's why they say teaching is learning twice.

birthday.title: Three birthdays
birthday.goal: Recall three birthdays without checking the calendar.
steps: Think of three people close to you.
Say or write each one's birthday.
Check them on the calendar and correct any you got wrong.
birthday.example: Mom: March 12. Charles: August 5. Lucy: November 30? The calendar says November 3.
birthday.done: when you've said the three dates and checked them.
birthday.why: Trying to recall and then correcting is the most effective way to make a fact stay.

handwrite.title: A handwritten note
handwrite.goal: Handwrite a short note for someone.
steps: Grab paper and a pencil or pen.
Write a short note to someone: thanks, encouragement or affection. At least three sentences.
Hand it over or leave it where they'll find it.
handwrite.example: “Thanks for taking me to the doctor on Tuesday. I don't say it much, but you made my day. I owe you a coffee.”
handwrite.done: when the note has reached its person.
handwrite.why: Writing by hand, with no spell-check or suggestions, makes you think through each sentence before you write it.

clock.title: How long to go?
clock.goal: Work out in your head how many minutes until your next meal.
steps: Look at the time just once.
Work out in your head how many minutes until your next meal.
Set a timer for that many minutes and see if it goes off right at mealtime.
clock.example: It's 10:35 and lunch is at 1:00. To 11 is 25 minutes, plus 2 hours: 145 minutes.
clock.done: when you've done the sum and checked it with the timer.
clock.why: Counting in hours and minutes is an everyday sum we nearly always leave to the phone.

onboarding.title: Switch off the autopilot
onboarding.p1: Pilots practice hand-flying so they don't lose the skill. Handfly does the same for what we now hand over to AI, GPS and calculators.
onboarding.howTitle: Here's how it works, every day:
onboarding.b1: You get a mission: something specific you do yourself, without AI, GPS or a calculator. It comes with steps and an example, and takes a few minutes.
onboarding.b2: You do it. Some happen right here in the app and mark themselves; others happen out in your day, and when you're done you tap “I did it!”.
onboarding.b3: You add real flight hours and move up in rank. If you save cards to review, the app asks them just before you'd forget.
onboarding.privacy: Everything stays on your phone. No accounts, ads or tracking.

about.title: About Handfly
about.origin: The name comes from aviation. Pilots who almost always fly on autopilot slowly lose the ability to fly by hand. That's why they practice hand-flying, even when they don't need to.
about.idea: The same happens to us with AI, GPS and calculators. They are great tools, but if we never do things without them, we stop knowing how. Handfly helps you practice on purpose, with tasks from your real life, so those skills are still there when you need them.
can: Help you build the habit of trying first before asking an AI.
Help you remember what you learn and the names of people you meet, using well-studied techniques.
Give you real practice finding your way, writing and doing math in everyday situations.
Show you, with honest data, how much you solve on your own and how much you hand off.
cannot: It won't make you smarter. No exercise has shown that, so be wary of anyone who promises it.
It doesn't improve memory "in general": it improves what you practice and very similar things.
It doesn't replace real-life practice. What counts is what you do outside the app.
It isn't a treatment. If you're worried about your memory or attention, talk to a health professional.
about.privacy: Everything you write (questions, names, notes, routes, texts) is stored only on this device. There are no accounts, no servers receiving your data, no ads and no usage analytics. You decide whether to download a backup and where to keep it.
about.ethics: There is no endless content. A session lasts 5 to 10 minutes and, when it ends, the app says goodbye and invites you to go practice. There's one optional reminder a day and no guilt-tripping messages. Your streak gets one rest day a week.
about.open: Handfly is free and open source under the MIT license. Every new module must explain why its practice helps in real life and cite the evidence behind it.
